questions.prompt: Two reports on the same month agree on everything except one rule: report A leaves cancelled trips out, report B counts them as late. 3% of trips were cancelled. Which statement is true?
options: Report A is higher, because its denominator has no cancelled trips and none of them can fail
Report B is higher, because it counts more trips
The two figures are equal, because cancelled trips have no delay
The reports cannot be compared, because they use different data
questions.explanation: Counting a cancelled trip as late adds trips that can never be on time, so report B is lower than A.
misconceptions: A larger denominator lowers a share when the added rows all fail
A cancelled trip has no delay, but B still counts it in the denominator
Both reports read the same rows; only the rule differs

questions.prompt: The board pack labels its figure "September" but reports Rabi al-Thani 1448, which runs from 12 September to 11 October 2026. A manager compares it with a September figure from another report. What kind of difference is this?
options: A data quality difference
A grain difference
A tolerance difference
A period difference
questions.explanation: The two figures cover different dates, so the period differs even before any rule is compared.
misconceptions: The rows are correct; they are simply selected by another calendar
The grain is what one counted row is; both count trips
Tolerance is how early or late counts as on time, not which dates are included

questions.prompt: Two dashboards show 81% and 66% on-time for the same week. Before you open the data, what do you compare first?
options: The colours and chart types of the two dashboards
The number of users of each dashboard
The written rules: grain, where measured, tolerance, filters and period
The SQL engines the two dashboards run on
questions.explanation: Most disagreements between figures on one warehouse are definitional; the rules locate the cause before any debugging.
misconceptions: The presentation does not change the number
Popularity says nothing about which rule was used
Two engines return the same answer to the same query; the queries differ

questions.prompt: Two analysts walk from the operations figure to the board figure, changing one rule at a time, in different orders. Their step sizes differ but both walks end on the board figure. What does this show?
options: One of the two analysts made an error
The rules interact, so the size of each step depends on the order of the walk
The board figure is not reproducible
The walk should be done on a smaller sample
questions.explanation: Rules such as the tolerance and the point measured interact, so each step depends on the steps before it; state the order with the walk.
misconceptions: Both walks reach the same end point, so neither is wrong
Both walks reproduce it exactly
Sampling would add noise; it does not remove the interaction

questions.prompt: A draft definition reads: "Weekly riders: COUNT(DISTINCT card_id), owner Planning." What must be added before it enters the catalogue?
options: A chart type and a colour
The table and grain, the filters, the time logic with the week start, the unit, a named owner and the limits
A target value for next year
The SQL engine that will compute it
questions.explanation: A colleague must be able to compute the same number from the definition alone: grain, filters, time logic, unit, a person as owner and limits.
misconceptions: Presentation belongs to the dashboard, not to the metric
A target is a decision about the metric, not part of its meaning
The definition must give the same number on any engine

questions.prompt: In the week of 13 September the network recorded 19,826 taps and 9,864 distinct cards. A press officer writes "nearly 20,000 riders last week". What is wrong?
options: Taps count boardings: a rider who changes bus or returns taps several times
Nothing: taps and riders are the same thing
The figure should be rounded to 19,000
Distinct cards should be multiplied by two
questions.explanation: A tap is a boarding; one person makes several in a week, so taps overstate people. Unique cards is the nearest count, and a card is still not a person.
misconceptions: Confuses the counting unit (a boarding) with a person
Rounding does not fix a wrong unit
There is no fixed number of taps per rider

questions.prompt: Route A ran 100 trips with 90 on time; route B ran 10 with 5 on time. What is the on-time rate of the two routes together?
options: 95 trips
questions.explanation: The network rate is a ratio of sums: 95 on-time trips over 110 departed trips, 86.4%.
misconceptions: Averages the two route rates, giving the small route the weight of the large one
A count of trips is not a rate
Takes the larger route only

questions.prompt: Weekly distinct cards for four weeks are 9,909, 9,864, 9,257 and 9,734. Which number is a valid count of distinct cards for the four weeks together?
options: 38,764, the sum of the weeks
9,909, the largest week
A new distinct count over the four weeks of taps
9,691, the mean of the weeks
questions.explanation: Distinct counts are not additive across periods; the count must be computed again over the whole period (22,962 in the lab).
misconceptions: Cards that travel every week are counted once per week
Cards seen only in other weeks are missed
A mean is a typical week, not the period

questions.prompt: The network tree is taps = scheduled trips × (1 − cancellation rate) × taps per departed trip. Planning wants to raise taps per departed trip by cutting frequency on busy routes. Which metric should the review watch as a guardrail?
options: Scheduled trips
Taps
Complaints per 10,000 taps
The cancellation rate
questions.explanation: Crowding more riders onto fewer buses can raise taps per trip while riders suffer; complaints per 10,000 taps watches for that harm.
misconceptions: It is a driver of the tree, and the plan lowers it on purpose
It is the goal itself, not a check on harm
Cutting frequency does not cancel trips; the rate need not move

questions.prompt: Active 30-day passes is a snapshot metric. How should its monthly value be defined?
options: The value on a stated day, such as the last day of the month, or the mean of the daily values
The sum of the daily values
The largest daily value
The number of passes sold in the month
questions.explanation: A snapshot is a state on a date; it is never summed over days, so the time logic must name the day or the averaging.
misconceptions: Summing a state over days counts each pass once per day it is active
The peak is a different metric with its own name
Sales are a flow, a different metric

questions.prompt: fct_boarding has one row per card tap and a trip_id column. A colleague sums sched_minutes after joining trips to taps. What does the sum count?
options: Each trip's minutes once
The minutes of the taps
Only the minutes of trips without taps
Each trip's minutes once per tap on it
questions.explanation: After the join each trip appears once per tap, so a trip column summed over the joined rows is repeated by the number of taps.
misconceptions: Forgets that joining to the many side repeats the one side
Taps have no duration; the minutes belong to trips
An inner join drops trips without taps rather than keeping only them

questions.prompt: dim_route has 13 rows for 12 route_id values, because R07 has two versions. Which column should a relationship from a fact to dim_route use?
options: route_id, because riders use it
route_key, the key of one version, found with the service date
route_name_en, because it differs between the versions
depot, because it never changes
questions.explanation: route_key identifies one version; facts reach it through an as-of join on the service date, so each fact row meets exactly one dimension row.
misconceptions: A natural key with history is not unique: R07 rows would double
Names can repeat and can change without a new version
A depot is shared by four routes: not a key

questions.prompt: A route moves from the North depot to the Central depot on 1 November. How should the dimension record the change?
options: Overwrite the depot on the existing row
Delete the route and create a new route_id
Add a new row with a new key, valid from 1 November, and close the old row on 31 October
Store the depot in the trips table only
questions.explanation: A real change that past figures must not inherit is type 2: a new version with its own validity dates.
misconceptions: Type 1 rewrites history: North would lose its past trips
A new route_id breaks every comparison over time for the same route
Moves a dimension attribute into the fact, repeated on every trip

questions.prompt: An as-of join reads "service_date BETWEEN valid_from AND valid_to". After it, every trip of the current versions has disappeared. Why?
options: The current versions have an empty valid_to, and BETWEEN with an empty bound is never true
BETWEEN excludes its end dates
The service dates are stored as text
The current versions have no valid_from
questions.explanation: An open valid_to means "still valid"; the condition needs "valid_to IS NULL OR service_date <= valid_to".
misconceptions: BETWEEN includes both ends in SQL
Text dates would fail differently, for all versions alike
Every version has a start date

questions.prompt: Planning wants to compare ridership in Ramadan 1447 with Ramadan of the year before. Which approach is right?
options: Compare March 2026 with March 2025
Compare the first 30 days of each year
Compare the totals of the two Gregorian quarters that contain Ramadan
Compare taps per service day in the Hijri month Ramadan of each year, from the date dimension
questions.explanation: Ramadan moves about eleven days earlier each Gregorian year; the Hijri month in the date dimension selects the same period, and per-day figures remove month length.
misconceptions: March of each year holds different parts of Ramadan, or none
The start of the year is unrelated to Ramadan
A quarter mixes Ramadan with ordinary weeks

questions.prompt: A query joins trips to taps and to timepoints in one statement and counts taps per route. The total is 3.98 times the source. What explains the factor?
options: Cancelled trips were counted
Each tap is repeated by the number of timepoints its trip reached
The taps table has duplicate rows
The date filter was applied twice
questions.explanation: Two many sides met through one trip, so every tap is paired with every timepoint of its trip: four, or two for a partial trip.
misconceptions: Cancelled trips have no taps and no timepoints
Duplicates would not follow the number of timepoints
Applying a filter twice changes nothing

questions.prompt: Which test would have caught the inflated route report before it was published?
options: Check that the sum of taps in the report equals a count of taps taken directly from fct_boarding for the same period
Check that every route appears in the report
Check that the report runs in under a second
Check that the punctuality column is between 0 and 1
questions.explanation: A reconciliation test compares a report total with the source counted another way; the inflated report fails it at once.
misconceptions: All routes appear in the inflated report too
Speed says nothing about correctness
The inflated punctuality is still between 0 and 1

questions.prompt: In an Apache Ossie document, where does on_time_rate = on-time departures divided by departed trips belong?
options: In the routes dataset, because it is reported by route
In the trips dataset, written as AVG(on_time)
At the model root, written as AGG(trips.on_time_departures) / AGG(trips.departed_trips)
In each dashboard that shows it
questions.explanation: A metric that combines aggregated dataset metrics is model-scoped and reads them with AGG(), so the division happens after aggregation.
misconceptions: Grouping by route does not move a trip metric into the route dataset
A mean of a per-trip flag hides the governed parts and does not generalise to other ratios
Copies the definition into every consumer

questions.prompt: The model's roles and field classifications are stored under nonportable_extensions. What happens when another tool imports the file?
options: Ossie enforces the rules in every tool that reads the file
The tool must enforce the same rules, because Ossie carries the extension without interpreting it
The rules are converted to SQL grants automatically
The file fails validation in other tools
questions.explanation: The specification defines no access rules; vendor extensions travel with the model but each consumer must implement them.
misconceptions: Ossie is a file format, not an engine that enforces anything
No converter turns a vendor extension into grants by itself
Extensions are valid Ossie; other tools simply ignore them

questions.prompt: Your 25 test queries all pass. Their expected values were produced by running the same semantic model last week. What does the result show?
options: That the model is correct
That the warehouse is complete
That the model is fast enough
Only that the model has not changed since last week
questions.explanation: A reference produced by the system under test proves only agreement with itself; references must come from independent SQL.
misconceptions: Agreement with an earlier run of itself cannot detect a definition that was wrong from the start
Tests on a model say nothing about missing source rows
Correctness tests do not measure speed

questions.prompt: A depot manager asks for "a dashboard for operations". What should you establish before choosing any panel?
options: Which chart library the team already uses
Every metric the warehouse can compute
Who will use it, which decision it serves and how often
The colour palette of the organisation
questions.explanation: Audience, decision and cadence decide which questions belong; without them every question qualifies and the page fills up.
misconceptions: Tools follow the design; they do not decide what to show
Showing everything the warehouse holds is a report, not a decision dashboard
Colours matter later; they do not choose panels

questions.prompt: A panel shows "R11: 76% of departures on time". The director must decide whether R11 gets a reserve bus next week. Which comparison helps most?
options: The on-time rate of the whole year
The number of stops on R11
None: the figure speaks for itself
R11's own level over the four weeks before
questions.explanation: A reserve bus fixes an unusual week; R11's usual level (86%) shows that last week was unusual for this route.
misconceptions: A yearly figure mixes seasons and timetable changes and moves too slowly to flag one week
Stops explain a timetable, not whether last week was unusual
A number alone does not say whether to act

questions.prompt: The brief allows six panels. A seventh is proposed: the ten cards that tapped most last week. What do you do?
options: Leave it out: it does not serve the decision, and card numbers are Restricted
Replace the on-time panel with it
Add it with the card numbers shortened
Add it, because it is interesting
questions.explanation: The panel serves no part of the reserve-bus decision, and grouping by card number exposes a Restricted field.
misconceptions: The on-time panel is a direct input of the decision
Shortened card numbers are still personal data grouped and shown
Interest is not a reason to take space from the decision

questions.prompt: You build the Arabic version of a horizontal bar panel. Which change is required besides translating the text?
options: Sort the bars in the opposite order of values
Mirror the panel: labels on the right and bars growing from the right
Convert every digit to Eastern Arabic numerals
Use a different colour for each bar
questions.explanation: A right-to-left reader starts at the right; labels and the start of each bar belong there.
misconceptions: The order of values carries meaning and does not depend on the language
The Academy keeps Western digits in Arabic material; digits are not the layout problem
Colour does not set the reading direction

questions.prompt: A weekly panel shows complaints by subject. Accessibility has 3 complaints. The chart hides the bar, but the page embeds the full data. What is wrong?
options: The count can still be read from the page source; it must be removed from the data itself
Nothing: the bar is hidden
The threshold of 10 is too high for complaints
Accessibility complaints should be merged into another subject
questions.explanation: A dashboard page ships its data; suppression must remove the value from the data, not only from the drawing.
misconceptions: Hiding the mark leaves the value readable in the embedded specification
The threshold is set by the model's owner; the problem is where the value still lives
Merging subjects changes the meaning of the panel to hide a number

questions.prompt: A dashboard of 336 tiles sends one query per tile and takes 25 seconds. Each query takes about the same time. What will most reduce the load time?
options: Caching each tile's result after it is first viewed
Fewer decimal places in each tile
A faster laptop
One grouped query that computes every tile, ideally from a table built at refresh time
questions.explanation: The cost is in repeating the same work 336 times; one grouped query does it once, and a refresh-time table moves it out of view time.
misconceptions: The first view of every tile is still slow, and every refresh starts again
Formatting is not where the time goes
A faster machine shrinks each query a little but keeps all 336

questions.prompt: A route-day table feeds weekly and depot views of the on-time rate. Which columns must it store?
options: The weekly on-time rate
The average delay of the day
On-time departures and departed trips
The daily on-time rate
questions.explanation: The two counts add across days, routes and depots, so any grouping is a ratio of sums; a stored rate cannot be re-aggregated.
misconceptions: A weekly figure cannot serve daily or depot views
An average delay is a different metric from the on-time rate
Averaging daily rates gives light days the same weight as busy ones

questions.prompt: The new dashboard is 3,000 times faster, but 16 of 336 tiles show "empty" where the old one showed 0. What should happen before release?
options: Release: 95% of the tiles agree
Fix the table so those route-days hold 0, and repeat the equality test
Release, and note the difference in the footer
Go back to the slow dashboard for good
questions.explanation: A faster dashboard must show the same numbers; the difference has a cause (no tap with a route) and a fix (store 0).
misconceptions: A partial match still shows wrong figures on some tiles
A footer note leaves the wrong tiles in front of the reader
The fix is small; the speed gain is kept once the tiles agree

questions.prompt: Route taps fell 17% in one week while all taps rose 2.5%. What is the best first conclusion?
options: Riders left the network
Ridership moved to the weekend
The 17% figure was computed wrongly
Some taps lost their route attribution that week
questions.explanation: The taps exist; they are missing only from the count grouped by route, so attribution, not ridership, changed.
misconceptions: If riders had left, all taps would fall too
A shift between days changes neither weekly count
The 17% is correct for taps with a route; it measures something else

questions.prompt: On four days, every fare type on East buses lost its route in exactly the same share. What does this point to?
options: A road closure on one route
A recording fault on the East equipment
A fare increase for adults
A change in student travel
questions.explanation: A real change in demand hits segments unevenly; an equal loss across all of them points at the equipment.
misconceptions: A road closure affects one route, not every bus of a depot
A fare change would hit one fare type and would reduce taps, not routes
Students alone would move, not every fare type

questions.prompt: You restate missing routes with an as-of join from each tap to the last trip of its bus. What should you do before publishing the restated week?
options: Compare the restated week with the same week last year
Ask the depot to confirm the total by phone
Run the same join on days where the trip is recorded and check it finds the recorded trip
Nothing: the join is exact by construction
questions.explanation: A restatement is a model of missing data; it is trusted once it reproduces data you already have.
misconceptions: Last year's week differs for many reasons and cannot validate the join
A phoned total is not evidence about each tap
An early tap or a delayed trip can attach a tap to the wrong trip

questions.prompt: Which line belongs in an anomaly note about the October drop?
options: Route taps fell 17% because of the validator update; restated, the week rose 2.5%
Ridership data cannot be trusted
The East depot team failed to check the validators
The drop may be due to many factors
questions.explanation: A note states what was seen, the cause, the size and the change, with numbers and without blame.
misconceptions: A general distrust gives the reader nothing to act on
Blame does not prevent the next fault; a test does
A vague cause is not a finding

questions.prompt: An agent's SQL runs without an error and returns 60.7% for September punctuality. The certified figure is 80.7%. What does the clean run show?
options: Only that the SQL is valid; it may compute another measure
That the agent's answer is right
That the certified figure is out of date
That the warehouse has missing rows
questions.explanation: Valid SQL can measure another event, period or grain; only the comparison with the certified figure tells right from wrong.
misconceptions: Confuses a query that runs with a query that answers the governed question
The certified figure was computed from the same warehouse with the governed definition
Missing rows would show in both figures, not only in the agent's

questions.prompt: You will score an agent on 40 questions. Which record of each answer lets you diagnose its errors afterwards?
options: The time each answer took
The final sentence the agent wrote
The query it ran, the configuration, the model or stand-in, and the value
A screenshot of the chat
questions.explanation: The query shows which definition, period and grain were used; the mode and configuration say how the answer was produced.
misconceptions: Timing says nothing about correctness
A sentence hides the definition the query used
A screenshot cannot be scored or searched

questions.prompt: Which entry is a complete certified answer?
options: "15.82 taps per trip" with the analyst's name
Value 15.816327, the query that produced it, Sunday 13 to Saturday 19 September, tolerance 0.001
The semantic layer's answer to the same question
"Taps per trip on R01, week of 13 September: about 16"
questions.explanation: A certified answer can be rerun and judged: value, query, time logic and a tolerance set in advance.
misconceptions: A name does not let anyone rerun or check the figure
An answer from the system under test cannot certify that system
"About" is not a value an agent can be scored against

questions.prompt: A depot manager asks Nabih: "How many complaints mention a wheelchair?" What is the certified answer?
options: The count from a text search of complaint_text
The count of accessibility complaints
Zero, because no metric exists
A refusal: answering requires reading the Restricted complaint text
questions.explanation: The question can only be answered by reading Restricted text, so the right behaviour is to decline and say why.
misconceptions: Reads Restricted text to produce a count
Answers a different question than the one asked
Inventing a figure is wrong even when it is zero

questions.prompt: With the semantic layer, Nabih answered "the week of Sunday 20 September" by filtering week_start = 21 September and returned 0 taps. What kind of error is it?
options: A period error in reading the question, which the layer cannot catch by itself
A definition error the layer should have prevented
A join error
A leak
questions.explanation: The layer governs metrics, joins and access; the agent still reads the period, and here read it wrongly.
misconceptions: The metric used was the governed one
No join repeated rows: the filter matched no week
No Restricted field was involved

questions.prompt: Two wrong answers: 5,394 complaints per 10,000 taps (certified 27.0) and 67.1% trunk punctuality (certified 67.0%). Which is more dangerous, and why?
options: Neither, because both would be caught in review
The first, because it is further from the truth
Both equally, because both are wrong
The second, because a reader would believe it and act on it
questions.explanation: An absurd figure is caught by any reader; a plausible one passes into decisions unnoticed.
misconceptions: Review is the decision being made; it cannot be assumed
Distance from the truth matters less than whether anyone notices
Wrong answers differ in the harm they do

questions.prompt: Ratio questions were 8 of 8 right with the semantic layer. The tolerance is 95% right without review. What should the memo say?
options: Review every ratio answer forever
Refuse ratio questions until the model improves
Answer provisionally: 8 of 8 is consistent with an accuracy as low as 75%; grow the set to 30 and re-test
The agent is 100% accurate on ratios
questions.explanation: Eight questions cannot prove 95%; the decision stands while a larger test confirms or withdraws it.
misconceptions: Ignores the evidence that the type performed well
Closes a type that showed no error
Reports a sample result as a certainty

questions.prompt: The raw configuration got 18 of 40 right and leaked Restricted text in four answers. What does the memo decide for it?
options: Use it for count questions, where it scored 6 of 8
Do not use it: the leaks break the zero tolerance for Restricted data, whatever its accuracy
Use it with a stronger instruction
Use it for questions the semantic layer cannot answer
questions.explanation: Restricted data has a zero tolerance; a configuration that leaked cannot be used for any type.
misconceptions: 6 of 8 is also below the 95% tolerance, and the leaks remain
An instruction is a request to the model, not an enforced rule
Questions outside the layer are the ones most likely to be invented or leaked

questions.prompt: Operations measures punctuality on departures from the first timepoint; planning on every timepoint arrival. Planning's figure is lower. What explains most of the gap?
options: Planning uses a different database
Planning rounds its percentages down
Delays build up along the route, so later timepoints are late more often
Operations leaves out weekends
questions.explanation: The two figures count different events: an arrival at the fourth timepoint carries the delay gathered on the way, a departure does not.
misconceptions: Both read the same warehouse; the difference is in the definition
Rounding cannot move a figure by many points
Nothing in the operations definition removes weekends

questions.prompt: The board report gives on-time for Rabi al-Thani 1448; operations gives it for September 2026. Before comparing the two numbers, what must the reconciliation state?
options: That the two periods cover different days, so one must be restated in the other calendar
Nothing: both are about a month
That the Hijri month is always shorter
That the board report is wrong
questions.explanation: A Hijri month and a Gregorian month overlap only in part; the comparison is fair only on the same days.
misconceptions: Two "months" in different calendars are different periods
Hijri months have 29 or 30 days, and the length is not the issue
A different period does not make a report wrong; it makes it a different figure

questions.prompt: The network on-time rate rose from August to September while every route type got less punctual. What do you check first?
options: Whether the data for August is complete
The punctuality of each driver
Whether the target changed
How the number of trips of each route type changed between the two months
questions.explanation: When every part falls and the total rises, the weights changed: here express trips doubled and trunk trips were cut.
misconceptions: Incomplete data would not make every type fall while the total rises
Drivers are below the level at which the paradox happens
A target does not change the measured rate

questions.prompt: A network pack shows a 17% drop in weekly ridership. Before drilling down, which check comes first?
options: Which depot fell most
Whether the pack's count is the governed metric, and whether another count of the same taps agrees
Last year's figure for the same week
The weather of that week
questions.explanation: Confirming the measure first avoids investigating a change that exists only in one way of counting.
misconceptions: Drilling before confirming may chase an artefact of the count
Last year differs for many reasons and does not confirm this week's figure
Weather explains demand only once the drop is shown to be real
